taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; broadly native from southeastern Canada through much of the U.S. to Mexico and South America.

evidence: USDA-derived Texas county/native-status data list native occurrences in Hays, Travis and Williamson Counties, among many others.
UT Plant Resources Center's Selected Central Texas Grasses includes M. schreberi for the NW Hays/Travis-centered regional flora.
target_zone_range.guardrail: County decision uses USDA-derived native county data; lawn/yard occurrence is not treated as native evidence by itself.

morphology.look_here_first: Forget the ornamental-muhly silhouette: nimblewill is low and weak. Look for decumbent much-branched stems that root at the lower nodes, short flat blades, and a narrow contracted panicle. That creeping/rooting habit separates it instantly from the two upright bunchgrasses.
diagnostic_traits: weak perennial grass with decumbent much-branched culms
lower stem nodes root and allow patches to spread
usually only 10–40 cm tall, occasionally taller
leaf blades short and flat, roughly 2–8 cm long and 1–4 mm wide
ligule minute, a short membrane/ciliolate membrane
panicle narrow and contracted, about 5–15 cm
panicle branches short and appressed to ascending

confusers.separator: Lindheimer muhly is a large upright fountain-form bunchgrass with long basal leaves and a huge feathery panicle.
Seep muhly is a compact upright tuft with threadlike leaves and open airy panicle; nimblewill creeps and roots at nodes.
Bermudagrass also creeps but has digitate fingerlike seedheads and obvious stolon/rhizome architecture unlike the narrow Muhlenbergia panicle.

installation_guardrail: May install under the user's blanket approval because strict PASS is complete.
